opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the easiest way to see it is that they answer two different questions. Multiple update frequencies answer *when* and *how fast* each part of the system learns. Knowledge transfer answers *how what one level learns gets to the others*. You really need both to have a working memory system.

If you think about the brain, there's this spectrum of timescales. Some processes adapt almost instantly, within the current context, and others consolidate slowly over hours, days, even longer. In Nested Learning we try to take that seriously. Instead of one model with one set of weights updated by one optimizer, you have a hierarchy of levels, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency. The fast levels absorb what's happening right now. The slower levels compress and store what stays useful across many contexts.

But if you stop there, you just have a bunch of components learning at different speeds in isolation, and that doesn't give you continual learning. The fast level would keep overwriting itself and forgetting, and the slow level would never benefit from what the fast level just discovered. So you need mechanisms for information to move between levels. That can happen through parameters, where one level's output initializes or conditions another. It can happen through gradients or a learned update rule. It can happen through backpropagation across levels. That's what I mean by knowledge transfer.

They're complementary because each one makes the other meaningful. Different frequencies create the separation: short-term versus long-term, plasticity versus stability. Knowledge transfer is the bridge that lets the system consolidate, moving things from fast, volatile memory into slower, more persistent memory, and letting the slow levels shape how the fast ones adapt. That's basically the memory consolidation story from neuroscience, just written as an optimization problem.

And when you look at existing architectures through this lens, a lot of what we already do turns out to be special cases. Attention is a fast, non-parametric memory over the current context. The MLP weights are a slow memory trained during pre-training. Even optimizers like momentum are small associative memories compressing the gradients. The weakness in current models is that the transfer between those levels is almost frozen after training: there's essentially no path for in-context knowledge to flow back into the persistent levels. That's why models seem to have something like anterograde amnesia. So the design goal is a continuum of frequencies, as in the continuum memory system idea, with real transfer paths between them, so the model can keep learning instead of only reacting.

r001.rationale: The response says knowledge transfer lets the slower level benefit from what the fast level discovers.

r002.rationale: It says slower levels compress and store useful information across contexts, but does not state that they focus on higher-level abstractions.

r003.rationale: It says fast levels absorb what is happening now and adapt, describing rapid adaptation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that these two pieces are really answering two halves of the same question, which is how a system can keep learning over time without either forgetting everything or freezing up.

The multiple update frequencies part comes from looking at the brain. You have different components of the system consolidating information at very different timescales. Some things update fast, almost every step, and they capture what's happening right now in the context. Other things update slowly, over many steps, and they hold onto more stable, abstract structure. In Nested Learning we make that explicit: you have a set of nested optimization problems, each one with its own context flow and its own update rate. The fast levels adapt quickly, the slow levels act as a kind of memory of memories. So that gives you a hierarchy of memory systems rather than one monolithic set of weights that gets hit by every gradient.

But just having levels that update at different speeds isn't enough on its own. If the fast levels learn something useful and it never makes its way into the slow levels, you've essentially built a system with great short-term memory and no way to consolidate. And if the slow levels change without any regard for what the fast levels have figured out, you get interference and forgetting. So the knowledge transfer piece is what connects the levels. Information has to flow upward, from the frequently updated components into the rarely updated ones, in a controlled way, so that what was learned in context eventually becomes part of the longer-term structure. And it has to flow downward too, so the slow, stable knowledge shapes how the fast components adapt.

That's why I say they're complementary. The frequencies define the structure, the separation of timescales. The transfer defines the dynamics, how learning actually moves across that structure. If you take one without the other, you either get a static hierarchy that doesn't consolidate, or a single-level learner that forgets. Put them together and you get something that looks a lot more like continual learning, where the model can keep absorbing new things in context while gradually compressing them into more permanent form.

And one thing I like about this framing is that it reinterprets a lot of what we already do. Backpropagation, optimizers with momentum, in-context learning in attention, these all look like different levels of the same nested system once you look at them through update frequency and information flow. So it's less about inventing a new mechanism and more about recognizing that the mechanisms were already there, and designing them deliberately rather than by accident.

r001.rationale: It says knowledge flows upward from frequently updated components so learning in context becomes part of the rarely updated levels’ longer-term structure.

r002.rationale: It describes slow levels as holding more stable, abstract structure.

r003.rationale: It says fast levels update frequently and adapt quickly to what is happening in context.

astra-6.text:
I think they address two different parts of the same problem. Multiple update frequencies let different parts of a system learn on different timescales. Some parts can adapt quickly to what is happening right now, while others change more slowly and preserve knowledge across many experiences. But having those different timescales is not sufficient by itself. You also need a way for knowledge to move between them.

For example, a fast-changing component might learn something useful from the current context. If that information never influences a slower-changing component, it may disappear when the context changes. At the same time, the slower component can provide structure that helps the faster component adapt more effectively.

So the update frequencies give you a way to separate immediate adaptation from longer-term retention, and knowledge transfer connects those processes. In Nested Learning, the interesting thing is how those learning processes interact—how what you learn quickly can improve what you retain, and how what you retain can improve what you learn next.

r001.rationale: The response says that what a fast-changing component learns can influence and improve what the slower component retains.

r002.rationale: It describes slower components as preserving knowledge and providing structure, but does not say they focus on higher-level abstractions of the data.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says fast-changing components adapt quickly to the current context and separates immediate adaptation from longer-term retention.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as answering two different questions. Multiple update frequencies tell us when different parts of a system should learn. Some parts need to respond quickly to the current context, while others should change more slowly, so they can preserve useful structure across many contexts. Knowledge transfer tells us how what is learned at one level becomes useful at another.

If you only have different update frequencies, you can end up with separate learning processes that don’t really benefit from one another. A fast process might discover something useful, but that discovery disappears unless there is a way to consolidate it into a slower process. And transfer goes the other way, too: slower knowledge can provide the structure that helps the faster process adapt efficiently.

So the complementarity is between specialization across timescales and communication across those timescales. In Nested Learning, we want to understand those together: how each learning process updates its own state, and how those updates influence the other learning processes in the system.

r001.rationale: It says a fast process can discover something useful and that consolidation lets a slower process benefit from it.

r002.rationale: It describes slower processes as preserving useful structure across contexts, but does not say they focus on higher-level abstractions of the data.

r003.rationale: It says fast processes respond quickly to the current context and adapt efficiently, conveying rapid adaptation.
